Over the last 2 years, retail sales have risen +$69 billion, or +10%.

Meanwhile, US consumer sentiment fell -1.8 points in early October, to 46.3, its 2nd-lowest in history.

Sentiment deteriorated most among lower-income consumers and those with smaller stock market portfolios.

The disconnect between what consumers think about the economy and how they spend is widening.

A lot of you were asking me where my $HIMS Longevity as a Service thesis was coming from

Naturally, management wasn’t talking about it

Here’s $HIMS Chief Medical Officer confirming this is what they’re up to
Anant Vinjamoori, MD @dranantmd · 16 Nov 2026, 04:30 SGT
Phase 1 of the longevity market is over.

Phase 1 was access arbitrage: sell a bigger lab panel or a trending molecule, and early adopters paid just to get in the door. Now access is commoditizing fast.

Phase 2 is when longevity becomes the baseline:

1. Raw data stops being a moat unless it changes a real clinical decision.
2. Starting a protocol is table stakes; proving that metabolism, strength, or sleep improved six months later is the product.
3. Static playbooks lose to learning systems where the 10,000th patient gets a smarter plan from what was measured across the first 9,999.

Monday at 12:00 PM PT, I'm on the HLTH Main Stage for "When Longevity Becomes the Baseline" with Dawn Mussallem, Naveen Jain, and Heather Landi.

If you're in Vegas this week, come join us.

The most interesting lesson Jensen Huang taught me

And gave PTSD to Google executives over from his leadership at $NVDA:

Was that if a critical material can be bought out for spare change eg. ~$400m (FY2028 Photonics-SOI revenue forecast for $SOI)

And trigger tens of billions in economic impact to competitors for not securing supply:

We're going to see game theory bottleneck supply procurement actually accelerate upstream through 2027, with or without him.

I see Morgan Stanley's list highlighting CCL, ABF, PCBs, optical module components as interesting.

However; I'd put it through my own narrower lens, especially focusing on smaller component cost chokepoints + bottlenecks that doesn't cost much to secure capacity over.

Deleveraging/negative sentiment is indiscriminately moving the theme up and down together, so hard to argue individual fundamentals at this point.

Reflecting on 2026, I also prob need to be more selective of companies entering 2027:

But there's going to be a lot of outsized opportunities in bottlenecks... as new architectures like NPO/CPO emerge across the ecosystem.

Guy @nosilverv · 10 Nov 2026, 18:30 SGT
Bunch of people losing their shit: how does he have the time to be Stripe's CEO AND read Brothers Karamazov?

Same people are surprised by how fast the most effective operators text back. I think all comes from the same place: short feedback loops, which build causal models.

If you act on ideas *fast* they don't stay as ideas long which means you get feedback on errors *fast*. This compounds over time and all your models become causal: they track the actual moving structures of the world. If you don't act on ideas fast they proliferate and become these big castles, these flights-of-fancy that might be barely tethered to reality.

05:44 SGTInvesting
Why a Stock Can Rally 20% and Still Be in a Stage 4 Downtrend

One of the biggest mistakes investors & traders make during market corrections is confusing a sharp rally with the beginning of a new uptrend.

A stock can decline 40%, rally 20%, and still remain in Stage 4.

Here's why these rallies often fail:

1. Declining Moving Averages
- The 30-week moving average (roughly equivalent to the 200-day SMA) is still pointing downward.
- A sharp rally into a declining moving average is often a countertrend move, not a sustainable uptrend.

2. Overhead Supply
Investors who bought at higher prices may use the recovery to exit near breakeven, creating selling pressure that limits the rally.

3. Lower Highs
- A stock can rally 20% and still fail below its previous swing high.
- As long as price continues making lower highs and lower lows, the broader downtrend remains intact.

4. No Constructive Base
Sustainable recoveries often require time to build a base.

A few things worth watching:
- Price stops making lower lows.
- Selling volume dries up during pullbacks.
- Weekly price action begins tightening.
- The 30-week moving average starts flattening.
- Relative strength improves.

So, what do I look for instead?

I prefer stocks that have completed their Stage 4 decline, established a constructive Stage 1 base, and are transitioning into Stage 2 with improving volume and relative strength.

My biggest takeaway:

You don't need to capture the first 20% of a recovery to generate meaningful returns.

Waiting for confirmation may mean missing the initial bounce, but it can also help avoid failed rallies and unnecessary losses.

The goal isn't to catch the exact bottom. It's to participate in the middle of a sustainable uptrend while managing risk.

Steve Yegge @Steve_Yegge · 15 Nov 2026, 02:27 SGT
I just finished talks about my software factories at two conferences. Afterwards a bunch of people came up and told me what they were surprised about. Here is a distillation of what people thought were hot takes from my two talks.

First hot take: I tell everyone to slow down. Most speakers go on about how fast they're going, but I strongly believe in pacing AI outputs to human speeds. I regularly tell AI-pilled CIOs and CTOs to chill: almost nobody is _actually_ going fast with AI. Engineering still moves at engineering speeds, and business moves even slower. The ones pushing too hard are starting to see downtime for it.

If you don't pace your AI to human speeds, everything starts breaking around you, even at small operations like my online video game. I only have about a dozen humans working with my factory, and only a few hundred active old-timer players in the community who get along well, and still, introducing AI has still been very rocky.

My agents have, at times, overwhelmed my players with features, my accountant with emails, my merge queue with tickets, and my machines with load. Agents have pissed off my admins, resulting in name-calling, they've made messes in the game, and they've launched broken OSS without permission. The list goes on.

I can get away with all this chaos because everyone involved in my operation is very forgiving. They're excited by the potential. But even so, I had to learn to slow down, real fast. And so that's what I preach.

Hot take #2: Should you buy a software factory? Do you even need one? No. You probably don't need one. Factories take an extraordinary amount of upkeep. They turn into garbage mountains unless you put a frightening amount of time and tokens into curating them. I had to burn my previous five factories down since it eventually became cheaper to rewrite them than to fix them. So I'm not out there advocating for software factories or swarms just yet. If you do want one, be aware that it is a significant commitment of both money and human leadership to keep one running.

Several people told me that I was the only one who stood up onstage, at either conference, and said Build, don't Buy. But my experience is that software factories grow to be highly bespoke to your domain. Mine is super tangled up with my game, and I think that's inevitable. Because the factory is not just building my product, it's supporting it too. It's a company in a box. And they're easy for Claude to build for you.

Third and arguably hottest take: Next year will have a lot of human/agent and agent/agent office drama, resulting from bringing in AI employees, and it will be gloriously funny, but also frustrating.

Many of you are already on this bandwagon, but everyone next year will have a personal chief-of-staff agent. Busy people, even hobbyists, will have whole entourages of helper agents. The hot take is that people will become so dependent on these little private entourages, that they'll bring them to work. Your people will talk to my people, etc. Whole protocols will emerge for private entourages negotiating work between humans, inside companies big and small.

Nearly all humans will wind up having to start working with AI employees next year, and it'll be the beginning of the biggest cultural change we've seen in a hundred years.

So that's the hot takes. Slow down. Only build a factory if you think you really need one. And focus on empowering yourself with your own agentic chief of staff (or team). Your entourage will define how you work with others, so start by perfecting how you work with them yourself.

@MichaelDell said it best.

Old GPUs are renting at a premium, and a HUGE premium at that.

The H100 started shipping in 2022, and it now rents for 58% more than it did a year ago. That isn't how a depreciating asset is supposed to behave.

This will keep happening as long as demand outruns supply.

AI cloud providers that locked in long-term contracts at last year's prices are leaving money on the table right now. Those contracts roll off eventually, though, and when they do, that capacity gets repriced 50%+ higher on hardware that's already been running for years.

The bear case for a GPU depreciating in 4 years is pretty much out of the picture now.

I'll keep saying this to anyone who needs to hear it: forget the temporary price action.
As long as demand and rental prices keep climbing, think long term, the way institutional players do.

They keep accumulating at these prices because they don't care if we go lower next week. THEY KNOW we go higher in a year.

US inflation is diverging from the Fed’s target:

US CPI Inflation has surged +30.2% since January 2020, to an all-time high.

This translates into an annualized inflation rate of +4.0% over this period.

Meanwhile, under a steady 2% annual inflation target, cumulative CPI growth would have been just +14.3%.

In other words, actual cumulative inflation is +15.9 percentage points above the target path, more than double the implied increase.

This comes as CPI has remained above 2% for 67 consecutive months.

The gap began widening again in March, as inflation has now remained above 3% for 7 consecutive months.

Asset owners are the only winners.

On the Nvidia situation:

Nvidia's board can still make things right.

It has now been 48 hours since Jensen Huang resigned from his role as CEO, President, and board member of Nvidia.

Meanwhile, a thorough investigation has not been completed, countless critical questions are unanswered, and one of the world's greatest CEOs was forced out before the full facts of the situation were established.

In fact, the US Attorney General, the CIA, the DNI, and members of the House Intelligence Committee have also suggested that the current evidence remains inconclusive regarding whether Jensen Huang was involved in an affair with a Chinese spy.

The reality is that Jensen Huang resigned in the heat of the moment and the board acted based on speculative information.

We believe Nvidia's board, $NVDA, has a duty to shareholders to openly acknowledge that Jensen Huang could return to the company, pending a thorough investigation.

What happens in a CEO's personal life should not automatically dictate his role in a company, particularly if an investigation fails to establish national security misconduct or other wrongdoing that warrants removal.

The right move is to acknowledge that Jensen Huang is innocent until proven guilty.

Nvidia's board must do this now. It is not too late.

Want to know how to avoid major drawdowns and improve your returns in the stock market?

Understanding Stan Weinstein's Stage Analysis is a great place to start. Every stock moves through 4 stages!

One of the most important lessons I've learned from Stan Weinstein's Stage Analysis is understanding where a stock stands in its market cycle and when to buy, hold, reduce exposure, or stay away.

The framework primarily uses the 30-week moving average (roughly equivalent to the 150-day SMA), price action, volume, and relative strength.

Stage 1: Basing / Accumulation

What does it look like?
- Usually forms after a prolonged Stage 4 downtrend
- Stock stops making consistent lower lows and starts trading sideways
- 30-week moving average begins to flatten
- Price moves above and below the flattening moving average
- Selling pressure decreases, and volume often dries up

What does it mean?
- The stock is trying to establish a bottom, but buyers haven't taken full control yet. This is where I start building my watchlist and looking for improving technicals, higher lows, and signs of accumulation.

- Remember, a stock falling 50-70% doesn't automatically make it a Stage 1 base. It needs time to stabilize and build a proper structure.

Stage 2: Advancing/Uptrend

What does it look like?
- Stock breaks out above its Stage 1 base
- Breakout ideally happens on expanding volume
- 30-week moving average starts sloping upward
- Higher highs and higher lows
- Relative strength improves against the broader market

What does it mean?
- Buyers are taking control, and institutional accumulation may be supporting the uptrend.

- This is my favorite stage to own growth stocks! I generally look for Stage 1 → Stage 2 breakouts and constructive pullbacks to rising moving averages.
- The goal isn't to buy at the absolute bottom but to participate when the stock starts showing evidence of a sustainable uptrend.

Stage 3 vs. Stage 4 - This is where a lot of us make mistakes!

Stage 3: Topping / Distribution

What does it look like?
- Usually forms after a prolonged Stage 2 advance
- Momentum slows, and price starts moving sideways
- 30-week moving average begins flattening
- Price repeatedly crosses above and below the moving average
- Breakouts start failing, and selling volume may increase
- Major support levels are still holding

What does it mean?
- The previous uptrend is losing momentum, and the stock may be going through distribution.

- Stage 3 doesn't automatically mean a crash is coming. Some stocks consolidate and resume their uptrends.

- For me, this is where I become cautious, tighten risk management, consider trimming positions, and avoid aggressively adding exposure.

Stage 4: Declining / Downtrend

What does it look like?
- Stock breaks below major support or its Stage 3 range
- 30-week moving average starts sloping downward
- Price trades below the declining moving average
- Lower highs and lower lows
- Short-term rallies often fail near declining moving averages

What does it mean?
- Sellers are in control, and the stock is in a downtrend.

- One of the biggest lessons I've learned is that technicals often reveal weakness before fundamentals do.

- A company can continue reporting strong earnings while its stock is entering Stage 4 because the market is already pricing in future expectations.

The biggest difference between Stage 3 and Stage 4:

Stage 3 = Sideways price action, flattening moving averages, potential distribution.
Stage 4 = Support breakdown, declining moving averages, established downtrend.

Another important thing to understand is that Stage 1 and Stage 3 can look very similar!

Both involve sideways price action and flattening moving averages. The difference is what happened before:

- Sideways consolidation after a prolonged decline could be Stage 1.
- Sideways consolidation after a major advance could be Stage 3.

My approach is simple:
Stage 1 - Build your watchlist and prepare.
Stage 2 - Look for opportunities to participate.
Stage 3 - Protect your gains and manage risk.
Stage 4 - Protect your capital and avoid weak downtrends.

Stage Analysis isn't perfect, but it's one of the most valuable frameworks I've learned in my investing and trading journey.

I use technicals to understand WHEN to participate and fundamentals to understand WHAT I'm buying.

Understanding these four stages can make a tremendous difference in how you navigate market cycles!

There's something that's been bothering me lately, and I feel it's worth addressing.

Many of you know that my account has become one of the go-to sources for educational content, especially during market drawdowns, along with technical and fundamental analysis. That's something I genuinely take pride in.

Throughout this year, I've spent countless hours researching, analyzing markets, and creating educational content using hand-sketched, whiteboard-style illustrations to simplify complex concepts.

Recently, several friends, including some well-known accounts in the trading and investing community, have reached out after noticing how closely certain educational content resembles my work, especially my hand-sketched visual presentations.

And I've noticed it myself, not just in the visuals, but also in how concepts are explained and presented.

I'm not here to point fingers, but it's genuinely disappointing to see work built on years of learning and countless hours of creativity being replicated with little originality.

Did I invent the hand-sketched style? Absolutely not. But I've developed my own approach, combining educational research with a consistent visual style many of you recognize today.

I have no problem with people taking inspiration from others. That's how we all learn and improve.

But take that inspiration and develop your own creative approach instead of simply copying someone else's work.

I'm an investor and trader first. Creating educational content is something I'm passionate about, and I'll continue sharing what I've learned to help others improve.

You might copy my work. You might imitate my style. But you can never copy the creativity, research, and thought process behind it.
